title: Configure and verify IPv4 and IPv6 addressing on a router interface
scenario: R1 connects to the LAN through GigabitEthernet0/0. Configure dual-stack addressing on that interface and bring it up. IPv4: 10.1.1.1/24. IPv6: 2001:db8:1::1/64.

tasks.text: Assign 10.1.1.1/24 to R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 and enable the interface
Assign IPv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64 to the same interface
Verify with 'show ip interface brief' and 'show ipv6 interface brief'

rubric.text: G0/0 line protocol is up (no shutdown)

config.R1:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:1::1/64
 no shutdown

solution.explanation: Layer 3 addressing requires the interface to be administratively up (no shutdown) with the line protocol up. Enabling IPv6 also auto-generates a link-local FE80::/10 address (modified EUI-64) on the interface.

references.label: Cisco: IPv6 Addressing and Basic Connectivity (IOS XE 17.x)

title: Configure VLANs and an 802.1Q trunk across two switches
scenario: SW1 and SW2 are connected on GigabitEthernet0/1. Create VLAN 10 (DATA) and VLAN 20 (SALES) on both switches, trunk the link between them with 802.1Q, and place SW1 FastEthernet0/1 in VLAN 10 as an access port.

tasks.text: Create VLAN 10 (DATA) and VLAN 20 (SALES) on both switches
Configure Gi0/1 as an 802.1Q trunk on both switches
Assign SW1 Fa0/1 to VLAN 10 as an access port

rubric.text: Fa0/1 is an access port in VLAN 10

config.SW1:
vlan 10
 name DATA
vlan 20
 name SALES
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
 switchport mode trunk
!
interface FastEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
config.SW2:
vlan 10
 name DATA
vlan 20
 name SALES
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
 switchport mode trunk

solution.explanation: VLANs must exist before assignment. The trunk carries tagged frames for VLANs 10 and 20; native VLAN frames stay untagged and the native VLAN must match on both ends. On platforms that support only 802.1Q the 'switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q' line is not required.

title: Configure and verify single-area OSPFv2
scenario: R1 (10.0.0.1/30) and R2 (10.0.0.2/30) connect on a point-to-point link. R1 has LAN 192.168.1.0/24 and R2 has LAN 192.168.2.0/24. Configure single-area OSPFv2 (area 0, process 1) so the two LANs can reach each other, using router IDs 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2.

startingConfigs.R1:
hostname R1
interface g0/0
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
interface g0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
startingConfigs.R2:
hostname R2
interface g0/0
 ip address 10.0.0.2 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
interface g0/1
 ip address 192.168.2.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown

tasks.text: Enable OSPF process 1 on R1 and R2
Advertise the connected networks into area 0 with correct wildcard masks
Set R1 router-id 1.1.1.1 and R2 router-id 2.2.2.2
Verify the neighbor adjacency reaches FULL

config.R1:
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
config.R2:
router ospf 1
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 network 192.168.2.0 0.0.0.255 area 0

solution.explanation: OSPF network statements use wildcard masks (inverse of the subnet mask). Both routers must agree on area and on hello/dead timers. On a point-to-point link there is no DR/BDR election and the adjacency proceeds to FULL. Setting an explicit router-id avoids it changing if interfaces flap.

references.label: Cisco: Enabling OSPFv2 on an Interface (IP Routing, IOS XE 17.x)

title: Configure inside source NAT overload (PAT)
scenario: R1 connects the inside LAN 192.168.1.0/24 (GigabitEthernet0/0) to the ISP through GigabitEthernet0/1 (203.0.113.2/30). Configure PAT (NAT overload) so all inside hosts share the outside interface address when reaching the internet.

startingConfigs.R1:
hostname R1
interface g0/0
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
interface g0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown

tasks.text: Mark G0/0 as 'ip nat inside' and G0/1 as 'ip nat outside'
Create ACL 1 permitting 192.168.1.0/24
Configure PAT (overload) using the outside interface

rubric.verifyCmd: show running-config | include ip nat inside source
rubric.verifyRegex: ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload

config.R1:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip nat outside
!
access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload

solution.explanation: PAT (NAT overload) maps many inside local addresses to one inside global address by tracking unique source ports. The ACL selects which inside source addresses get translated. Verify with 'show ip nat translations' and 'show ip nat statistics'.

references.label: Cisco: NAT Configuration Guide (Catalyst 9000, IOS XE 17)

title: Create and apply a named extended ACL
scenario: On R1, block host 192.168.1.10 from reaching the server subnet 10.0.0.0/24 over HTTP (TCP 80), while allowing all other traffic. Apply the policy inbound on G0/0, the interface facing 192.168.1.0/24.

startingConfigs.R1:
hostname R1
interface g0/0
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
interface g0/1
 ip address 10.0.0.254 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown

tasks.text: Create a named extended ACL called BLOCK_WEB
Deny TCP from host 192.168.1.10 to 10.0.0.0/24 on port 80
Permit all other IP traffic
Apply the ACL inbound on G0/0

rubric.text: Deny rule for host to web server present
Permit ip any any present after the deny

config.R1:
ip access-list extended BLOCK_WEB
 deny tcp host 192.168.1.10 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 eq 80
 permit ip any any
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip access-group BLOCK_WEB in

solution.explanation: Extended ACLs match source, destination, protocol and port, and should be placed close to the source. Order matters: the specific deny must come before the broad permit. The implicit 'deny any' at the end of every ACL is why an explicit 'permit ip any any' is needed to allow the rest of the traffic.

references.label: Cisco: IP Access List Overview (Security Config Guide, IOS XE)

title: Interpret a JSON response from a REST API (GET)

tasks.text: State the value of the 'hostname' key
State how many objects are in the 'interfaces' array
State the 'name' of the first interface object

config.answers: hostname = "R1"; interfaces array length = 2; interfaces[0].name = "GigabitEthernet0/0" (enabled true); interfaces[1].name = "GigabitEthernet0/1" (enabled false)

solution.explanation: JSON objects use { } with "key": value pairs; arrays use [ ] and are zero-indexed. A REST 'Read' is an HTTP GET. RESTCONF returns YANG-modeled data encoded as JSON (or XML), which is exactly this kind of structure.

references.label: Cisco: RESTCONF Protocol (data encoding, IOS XE)
